These findings have crucial implications for understanding the dynamics of coronal mass ejections and should encourage researchers to examine this phenomenon through the analysis of actual coronal images.

A novel arrangement of a magnetically-trapped evaporative cooling device has been designed and implemented, with all key components integrated onto a single silicon chip. This integrated design offers a 10 times efficiency improvement over conventional models due to a reduced magnetic field propagation area and optimization of evaporation zones. The intended application is the development of an array of optical clocks using this compact and efficient mini-magnet trap.

A theoretical model is proposed to address the low luminosity of supermassive black holes such as Sgr A* and M87*. It is postulated that a power-law distribution of black hole masses, in conjunction with a relationship between their masses and accretion rates, could result in the observed luminosity levels. It is further hypothesized that black hole masses are a product of their initial masses and a factor that depends on their accretion rates to a power of approximately 2.4. This explains the low luminosity of M87* due to its high intrinsic variability amplitude, as well as the low luminosity of Sgr A* resulting from its high intrinsic variability amplitude.

We investigate the impact of neutral atom motion parallel to a boundary on single-photon emission processes. This includes examining how motion modifies spontaneous emission, beaming, and beaming, as well as the emission of pulled photons. Furthermore, we discuss the special case of a stationary mirror and provide examples of how an atom's trajectory influences these phenomena.

The minimax principle's implication for solution existence in a variety of problems has been well-documented. This paper focuses on its connection to critical point theory, specifically how the concept of essential components of critical sets relates to the minimax value. We provide a comprehensive example that illustrates a scenario where the standard minimax value-solution existence link fails due to an essential component with unusual properties.

This research presents a novel framework that integrates a handwritten text recognizer with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance the optical character recognition process on degraded document images. By incorporating a classifier into the GAN structure, the model is trained to minimize generation errors and thereby enhance the overall quality of the produced images. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework is more effective than traditional data augmentation methods and that the Adversarial Network approach can be directly applied to degrade digital images, without the need for physical re-scanning.

Text extraction from ID cards is a complex task, particularly for low-resource languages, which often suffer from suboptimal performance in existing methods. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework combining an optical character recognition (OCR) system and a natural language processing (NLP) approach to extract information from Indonesian ID cards. The NLP component of our system is trained to recognize and correct sub-optimal OCR outputs, ensuring high accuracy. The effectiveness of our proposed framework is demonstrated by its superior performance on the publicly available character-level dataset, as well as its successful application in real-world scenarios, including physical ID card processing andGr8f Indonesia's ID card digitalization project.

A key challenge in orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) systems is channel estimation, especially in scenarios with large delay spreads. Traditional methods, like pilot-based estimation, often struggle to maintain accuracy when the channel dispersion is limited. This paper explores how LSTM and gated recurrent unit (GRU) learning machines can be utilized in channel estimation. It first develops an algorithm that estimates the channel impulse response, followed by a demonstration of the model's ability to adapt to varying channel conditions and accurately recover the channel coefficients. Simulation results show that LSTM and GRU-based channel estimation outperform traditional methods, particularly in high mobility situations. Additionally, these models exhibit flexibility in adapting to different system parameters. This research also examines how hyperparameter selection impacts their generalization capabilities and compares their complexity with conventional algorithms.

Astronomical images are frequently affected by various factors, including the quality of telescopes, which can result in low-resolution images. To improve the clarity of astronomical images, we employ deep learning techniques, specifically supervised learning with data enhancement to gather more training samples. We compare two methods of data enhancement and find that although they produce similar results when used individually, combining them yields the best outcome. This study also examines the effectiveness of these methods on images from various astronomical fields, including extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology.

Optimizing the parameters of a neural network involves navigating a vast and irregular search space to reach a local minimum that corresponds to the network's optimal performance. However, traditional optimization techniques like gradient descent are not always effective in this context. We have developed an iterative algorithm to optimize the parameters of a neural network in a sequential manner, drawing inspiration from non-preemptive job scheduling on parallel machines. This algorithm avoids overfitting the network and can replicate the network's behavior outside the dataset used for training. Additionally, it enables the simultaneous optimization of multiple networks by finding a near-optimal scheduling approach that minimizes the overall computation time.

In 2019, the ECFA established an Early Career Researcher's (ECR) working group, and by 2020, it had launched an official panel. During its first year of operation, the panel held three meetings either in person at ECFA meetings or via online platforms. Its primary objectives are to establish the panel's organizational framework, define its operating procedures, and in future years, present awards at annual ECFA meetings.

This research demonstrates line waves in an integrated optical domain using a grapheme patch design that enables their efficient propagation. A specific arrangement of a graphene and dielectric patch interface within a silicon photonic waveguide platform enables the localization and propagation of a line mode. Furthermore, a silicon photonic Y-junction design incorporating the graphene patch allows for the successful splitting and propagation of line waves. Our results show that the presence of the graphene increases propagation losses by 10-15 dB/cm; however, these losses can be mitigated by optimizing the photonic waveguide dimensions. Our findings highlight the potential of utilizing graphene patches to interface with line waves for photonic and plasmonic interconnect applications.

This study presents a novel approach to multi-human multi-robot interaction through a Federated Learning framework. Focused on multi-robot manipulation tasks where humans and robots collaborate to complete tasks, our research explores how Federated Learning can facilitate collaborative interaction between humans and robots. The key benefit of employing Federated Learning in this context is its ability to protect individual training data, and its capacity to gather diverse interaction data without the need to collect or transfer sensitive information. To address the challenge of capturing interaction data, our research develops a novel data collection system incorporating a network of cameras and a centralized data collection server. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in producing high-quality interaction data and achieving a central model with minimal loss in training performance, compared to the traditional model trained on aggregated data.

A novel method of bias-reduced estimation is introduced, which doesn't require predefined aspects to be smooth. This method leverages the profile likelihood to decrease bias to an even higher order. Furthermore, it can be applied in a flexible way to various bias-reduced estimators, including the maximum likelihood estimator. This method is also applicable to situations involving incidental parameters and is demonstrated through the example of regression with random effects. Our method improves upon existing bias reduction techniques, such as the Lindstrom-Bates estimator, which only achieves bias reduction of order O(n^(-1)).

A novel approach called knowledge graph link prediction, which uses implicit
knowledge from a graph, has the potential to uncover hidden patterns.
Our solution builds on recent advances in relation extraction and uses newly
introduced concepts of entity representation and scoring to determine whether a
specific entity link exists. To create effective entity representations, we use
both the existing graph structure and external sources like text documents. To
assess the reliability of predicted links, we introduce a scoring mechanism
that considers multiple potential relationships for each entity. This method has
demonstrated superior performance in experiments and outperformed existing
link prediction methods that use only graph structure in a linear fashion.

In the context of three-flavor massive type-IIB SUGRA with the relevant effective scalar Lagrangian, we investigate the DEYE sphere, DEYE sphere, and DEYE sphere masses resulting from DEYE sphere fluctuations of relevant scalar fields in the context of DEYE sphere mass. Similar to the previously discussed DEYE sphere, we also examine DEYE sphere, DEYE sphere, and DEYE sphere masses resulting from DEYE sphere fluctuations in the presence of a baryonic potential. It's observed that the four DEYE sphere, four DEYE sphere, and three DEYE sphere Debye masses are interrelated. Moreover, we derived an analytical expression for the DEYE sphere, four DEYE sphere, and DEYE sphere Debye masses.

A study of the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 was conducted using neutron diffraction, and both compounds were found to have a unique magnetic structure with two distinct Ru ions (Ru1 and Ru2). However, unlike Tb3RuO7, in which the magnetic structures of the Tb and Ru ions are intertwined, Nd3RuO7 exhibits separate magnetic structures for the Nd and Ru ions. Furthermore, while Tb3RuO7 has been found to have a spin gap, this phenomenon is not present in Nd3RuO7.

A novel local-functional model is proposed to enhance the efficiency of neural networks in processing low-dimensional signals by reducing the dimensionality of the data. The model is applied to neural networks, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through a comparison of two instances: one with a local-functional representation and another without. When used on synthetic data, the local-functional model demonstrates better generalization capabilities. The model also successfully achieves dimensionality reduction in real-world data sets, and its performance iscomparable to traditional neural networks. However, when tested on data suitable for k-nearest neighbor classification, the local-functional model demonstrates superior performance.

We introduce a novel semi-generative model that incorporates both the causes and effects of a target variable, enabling practitioners to both interpret data and make accurate predictions. This model assumes that the effect is a direct result of the cause acting on the target, with unobserved noise also influencing the process. By treating the cause as latent, we employ a variational approach to both interpret the data and preserve predictive capabilities. This variational method introduces a new type of regularizer that takes into account the causal relationships between the target, cause, and effect. This variational model is then compared with other established methods for interpreting effects, including congeneric and orthogonal models. Additionally, the effectiveness of the model is further enhanced by introducing a modular variational model that treats the cause and effect as a combination of their interdependent and independent interactions with the target, with regularizer terms that reflect this modularity assumption. This variational model is subsequently compared with the corresponding generative model. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed models in a range of practical tasks.

Recent research in deep learning has highlighted the significance of geometric properties.
By analyzing these characteristics, algorithms and architectures can be refined.
To understand geometric properties, metrics must be defined, which in turn require linear algebraic structures such as vector spaces and algebra.
The study of deep geometric properties has gained momentum due to advancements in this field.
This review will re-examine fundamental concepts within deep learning from a geometric perspective, focusing on their underlying algebraic structures.

The research focuses on the distribution of lattice basins of attraction for a third-order field embedded in a 16-dimensional space representing its three possible fully reduced forms. A specific subclass of cubic fields with a particular characteristic property is analyzed. It has been observed that the lattice's characteristics significantly impact the behavior of the basins of attraction. By altering the radicands within a specific subgroup of cubic fields, a transition from symmetric to highly asymmetrical boundary shapes can be induced.

Several methods exist for uncovering the underlying mechanisms of deep neural networks, including methods that reveal how inputs progress through layers and methods for pinpointing feature relevance across the network. We combine these approaches by using layerwise relevance propagation to build on a ReNN's initial state in order to develop a novel supervised method called RNN-ReLP. Experiments conducted with RNN-ReLP demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying key initial states that are relevant to classification tasks in datasets such as IMDB, YouTube-Comments, and IMDB-MV. Its performance matches or surpasses that of carefully engineered initial states, thus validating the model. Furthermore, analysis of learned states shows their capacity to capture nuanced aspects of text data, including sentiment and movie genre.

A parameter 'r' introduces a new family of Stirling numbers of the second kind, which classify 'r-unordered' partitions of a set of size 'n' into non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least 'r' elements. We create a corresponding number triangle for this family, which we use to develop a new recursive formula, establish key properties, and identify additional relationships within this family.

We have developed a comprehensive theoretical framework for classifying material domains based on their microscopic symmetries. Our framework is applied to multi-layered materials, which exhibit layer permutation and shift symmetries. The definition of a material domain encompasses all irreducible sets of unique layer configurations. We identify four categories of irreducible domains based on the presence of these symmetries. Each category is characterized by specific properties and examples. Furthermore, our theory explains the emergence of a topological interface charge in terms of broken symmetries and demonstrates its relationship with layer stoichiometry.

A model of a particle on a generic d-dimensional manifold of diameter $D$ is considered, with its momentum defined up to a maximum level related to a classical wave with length equal to $D$. This state model is utilized to calculate key properties of the particle, including its energy, with emphasis placed on understanding how the particle's properties change with its mobility. Additionally, the role of the particle's mobility is explored from a fundamental perspective.

We introduce a novel method to train affine coupling layers for Monte Carlo simulations by utilizing complex numbers. This technique enhances sampling efficiency by doubling the flow's capacity without increasing parameter count. Additionally, it boosts the efficiency of rule-based integrators by enabling a greater step size to be used for a given simulation accuracy.

A novel approach to understanding the relationship between the masses of the top and bottom quarks is proposed within the context of an SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y gauge theory. This model incorporates two complex doublets and additional fermion singlets for the first and third generation quarks, utilizing a discrete Z_2 symmetry to prevent unwanted operator interactions. By way of flavor U(1)_F symmetry breaking, a mass difference between the two quark families is introduced, with the ultimate mass difference attributed to the weak interaction. To account for this difference, the symmetry is broken at a scale of approximately 10^11 GeV. A mechanism involving higher dimensional operators is suggested to break the Z_2 symmetry, allowing for the explanation of a flavor singlet interaction between the Higgs doublets. This model also provides an explanation for the smallness of the neutrino mass through the seesaw mechanism, with the required scale of right-handed neutrino interaction being in the range 10^11 GeV, thus offering the potential to test the theory's validity.

Virtual Machine Performance Counters (VPPMs) have become a valuable tool for system administrators to assess the performance of virtual machines. However, VPPMs can also be exploited by malicious users to facilitate denial-of-service attacks, allowing them to overload either the host system or allocated resources. In this paper, we present an innovative approach for simulating VPPMs in a secure manner, preventing malicious overloading while accurately reflecting real performance behavior. Our method involves a custom resource allocation policy that uses a first-come, first-served mechanism to distribute physical resources among competing VPPMs. Additionally, we develop a set of formulas for countering common performance optimization techniques. Through performance testing, we validate that our VPPM simulator effectively matches the performance characteristics of hardware-based VPPMs and prevents malicious overloading even under extreme conditions.

The performance of large, pre-trained language models has been widely recognized, 
but their adaptability to new, low-resource languages has not been thoroughly 
examined. This research delves into the effectiveness of pre-trained models in 
translating from a novel, low-resource language to a resource-rich one. 
Specifically, it investigates whether the choice of pre-training corpus, 
particularly in terms of corpus size and complexity, impacts the models' 
performance in this context. Furthermore, the study compares different 
fine-tuning strategies and pre-training objectives to assess their effectiveness 
in improving translation performance. The findings suggest that pre-training on 
a larger and more diverse corpus yields pre-trained models that are more 
resilient to variation in data and better suited for cross-lingual translation 
tasks, regardless of the specific pre-training objective employed.

To understand how a rapidly rotating star's core breaks up and forms a binary system, researchers have used simulations with advanced codes that model self-gravitating fluids. This study examines how energy is conserved and distributed during such a event, specifically looking at the conditions of a rapidly rotating, uniformly dense star. When a binary forms, data shows the mass of the binary system has more kinetic energy, while the remaining mass has more kinetic energy, relative to their respective gravitational energy. This trend has also been observed in more complex, realistically composed stellar models.

We introduce an advanced kernel-based function, the m-arithmetic kernel (m-ar-K), which enhances the effectiveness of unsupervised dimensionality reduction methods. These methods surpass the performance of traditional techniques like the Gaussian and Laplacian kernels. Using m-ar-K function-based kernels significantly improves the accuracy of Anomaly Detection with Unsupervised Learning.

A recent finding by Moshkovitz and Reingold showed that a substantial gap exists between the power of CPT and PTIME. We propose an alternative scenario in which this relationship is clarified by considering a situation where there's a considerable difference between PTIME and CPT only if there's an extremely efficient connection between CPT and EPC. Specifically, such a connection would imply that CPT can be expanded to include more powerful computational resources through multiple levels of parallel access. This would result in the inclusion of larger classes, such as NEXP, within an extended version of CPT that includes this new computational capability.

A commutative, unital ring $R$ with nilpotent elements has the property that for any ideal generated by a single nilpotent element, there's a corresponding minimal ideal that's also principal and generated by a nilpotent element. It has been an open question whether such a ring must have only one nilpotent element up to equivalence. We've found that for three-nilpotent elements, the answer is indeed affirmative, but for any quadruple-nilpotent element, counterexamples can be constructed.

Social media platforms have become a primary source of public discourse, allowing anyone to share their opinions freely. Thisopportunity has led to both positive outcomes, such as heightened public awareness about critical issues like racism and sexism, and negative consequences, such as the proliferation of hate speech. Despite its significance in understanding public sentiment, research in this area has been limited due to the complexity of classifying minified and complex social media messages. This study addresses this gap by introducing a comprehensive framework that categorizes individual Facebook posts into distinct, granular classes. The framework is paired with a proprietary dataset comprising over 100,000 posts. Initially, we train a model to identify the main narrative of each post and its sentiment. Subsequently, we develop a second model that classifies the post into one of 12 distinct categories based on the post's content and the identified narrative. This fine-grained classification enables a more nuanced exploration of public debates on social media.

This research introduces a novel system for event detection in real-world images that spans multiple temporal frames and spatial resolutions. Unlike existing methods, which assume a uniform spatial resolution for real-time image analysis, our approach recognizes the need for multiple resolutions by catering to the distinct characteristics of spatio-temporal events. This capability is particularly beneficial for applications like traffic monitoring, where we can simultaneously analyze images from a surveillance camera at different levels of spatial detail. Furthermore, our approach accounts for the variability in event duration, allowing us to process short and long sequences without requiring extensive training data. This research also explores the feasibility of processing such events on streaming devices, such as the Raspberry Pi 3, by developing a lightweight neural network. Experimental results using a dataset of a traffic intersection validate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting vehicles at various scales.

The number of usable CMB lensing measurements has increased with advances in observational capabilities, and these measurements are becoming an essential tool for CMB-based cosmology. Since the CMB lensing power spectrum is not influenced by galaxy bias, it can be employed to investigate the relationship between the lensing and galaxy distributions as an indicator of galaxy bias. This paper investigates the feasibility of using the lensing power spectrum as a measure of galaxy bias in combination with large-scale structure (LSS) data from the Cosmicflows-3 catalog of galaxy distances and LSS power spectrum data up to a wavenumber of approximately 1.5, which is expected to be possible with future observations. Our research finds that the lensing power spectrum has a minimal impact on our current estimates of galaxy bias but is likely to be useful in the forthcoming Cosmicflows-3 revision and the next generation of surveys.

The main challenge in deep learning model verification lies in guaranteeing that a model will perform accurately under the worst-case scenarios. Traditional approaches to model testing involve analyzing regions in the input space, which can be computationally expensive and limit the model's efficiency. A more practical method is needed to verify models in real-time applications. This paper introduces a novel framework that enhances a model's input space analysis by applying second-order Taylor approximations. By doing so, our framework can regionally certify models against worst-case perturbations. We can control the level of accuracy in our verification by adjusting the range of input regions. This approach is supported by theoretical guarantees that the verification results are within a known bound. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework with case studies that verify the robustness of models against various types of adversarial attacks.

The spread of false information on social platforms poses a major threat to online communities. Understanding the factors that influence the growth, decline, and final intensity of rumors during online discussions could help in developing more effective strategies to combat the spread of false information. In this study, we analyze peak and decay patterns in a large dataset consisting of 1178 rumors collected during the 2018 Beijing International Consumer Electronics Show. By examining peak and decay patterns within online discussions about specific products, we discovered the following key findings: (1) precursor features and location data have a significant impact on both the peak and decay patterns of rumors; (2) the decay patterns of different types of rumors are distinct and can be modeled using a Cauchy function with varied parameters for each; and (3) the initial decay pattern is often more complex than the peak pattern.

In our research, we introduce a novel approach to hyperspectral pixel classification that leverages dimensionality reduction techniques. Our framework employs an end-to-end learning process where a neural network is trained to minimize the discrepancy between predicted labels and actual class information. To assess the efficacy of this approach, we conducted a large-scale experiment involving 150 distinct classification scenarios and 15 different dimensionality reduction methods. Our results indicate that methods such as supervised manifold projection and margin-based spectral balancing out traditional dimensionality reduction techniques in terms of classification performance. Furthermore, our experimental findings reveal that the proposed end-to-end learning method consistently surpasses existing pixel-wise classification methods.

Several methods exist for compressing deep neural networks, including quantization, pruning and knowledge distillation, but these techniques often have drawbacks such as requiring memory for storing parameters or producing a network that generalizes poorly. This paper presents a novel compression approach that utilizes compressive learning, which effectively reduces the size of DNN parameters by transforming them into a compact form through partial differential equations. The method's benefits include improved generalization and reduced parameter storage requirements. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach not only achieves superior generalization but also surpasses existing compression methods in terms of accuracy, outperforming them by up to 4% while requiring less parameters for storage.

We introduce ProCS, a Protein Contact-Smoothening approach that refines crude protein structures by leveraging high-throughput experiments like FRET, which measure the distance between amino acids in proteins. Recent research has utilized discrete differential geometry to develop contact-smoother methods that can be applied to coarse-grained protein structures. However, these methods are constrained by the reliability of input data and are limited by the lack of information about protein's energy dynamics. To overcome these limitations, ProCS incorporates the reliability of high-throughput data and utilizes a potential energy function to supplement discrete differential geometry, ultimately producing refined structures that closely match the experiments. ProCS demonstrates remarkable accuracy in accurately reconstructing crude protein structures, even with limited or noisy data.

Optimizing generative models is heavily influenced by the loss function employed, and research has demonstrated that even slight modifications can lead to significant differences in performance. This research investigates whether models trained with lesser-known loss functions, such as KL Divergence, might outperform those trained with more established methods. To address this issue, we introduce a new research direction - loss function exploration - to assess the performance of under-explored loss functions. This involves fine-tuning pre-trained generators using different loss functions and comparing their effectiveness. Our study focuses on three generators and 18 loss functions, revealing that KL Divergence may actually result in poorer fine-tuning outcomes compared to other loss functions. Consequently, future research should prioritize exploring the efficacy of lesser-known loss functions in transfer learning scenarios.

The parquet amplitude's conservation, crossing symmetry, and analyticity properties are investigated. Various approximations to the parquet amplitude exhibit neither conservation nor crossing symmetry. A unique derivation from the Hamiltonian provides the parquet amplitude a consistent approach that satisfies conservation requirements. This amplitude's crossing symmetry fails at a specific energy threshold. Both the Hamiltonian-based and standard parquet amplitude formulations converge to the same result within a certain energy regime.

Studies of electronic correlations in two-dimensional materials, such as titanium disulfide, are crucial to understanding their behavior when they form a charge-density-wave pattern. Research using a micromechanical device has shown that excitations in monolayer titanium disulfide can occur without forming a superconducting state, and instead lead to an exciton condensate. This is supported by evidence showing a distinct transition temperature dependent on device size, and specific properties formed as a result of excitation, such as chiral currents and energy gaps, that match theoretical predictions.

In text-based risk reporting systems, dispatchers receive various event types from users via different channels and extract essential information for further processing.  Current dispatchers receive a basic training on how to gather this critical data, but this instruction is inconsistent and not specifically tailored to each category of risk.  To address this knowledge gap, we developed a set of guidelines called Knowledgeable Dispatching, which outlines the crucial information needed from users for effective risk reporting.  To promote standardization in gathering user information, we manually created annotated guidelines for four common risk categories - police, fire, medical, and other - associated with the BERTa risk reporting system.  Our research demonstrates that providing dispatchers with these categories and associated requirements during training results in a more accurate and comprehensive data collection from citizens.

We have computed corrections to two key properties of a superconductor near a node in the gap: its magnetization and heat capacity. These calculations consider a specific type of scattering and topological features of the surface. Our analysis reveals that for certain scattering types, the magnetization correction remains unaffected while the heat capacity behaves differently. The findings also show that the heat capacity can change sign due to different topological properties of the surface. The study involved numerical methods to confirm initial results obtained through initial approximations.

A novel, semi-supervised active learning method based on minimax entropy is proposed, aiming to enhance the efficiency of unlabeled data annotation in automated sample collection processes. The existing approaches to active learning often focus on either uncertainty or diversity in label acquisition, however, our method minimizes both factors by leveraging a semi-supervised framework. The selection of training samples is governed by two entropies - one for the labeled and one for the unlabeled data sets. By incorporating a semi-supervised paradigm, reduced entropy for both sets can be achieved. The experiment results indicate that our algorithm outperforms existing uncertainty and diversity-based active learning methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Music's ability to evoke emotions through timbre is a crucial aspect,
particularly in popular songs, where the emotional impact of vocals and
instruments is often amplified by songwriters and producers who draw
inspiration from and pay homage to their musical predecessors. To examine
the evolution of timbre in popular songs, we developed a system that
classifies songs into genres, detects genres within a single song, and
measures timbre similarity. We then used this method to analyze the
similarity of top 100 songs from each decade in the US, spanning 1958 to
2018. The results show distinct patterns of timbre similarity across
decades, with certain genres, such as disco and hip-hop, exhibiting
notable characteristics.

A novel class of processes, characterized by reinforcement, examines how the cardinality of blocks changes over time, revealing that, despite initial complexity, the process exhibits plateaus that occur at a rate that can be associated with the inverse of a power function, specifically with the block size. This property holds across a range of block sizes, leading to the conclusion that, for any given process in the considered class, it is consistent with established theoretical frameworks.

This paper proposes an approach to understanding meaning in terms of reasoning, rooted in the work of Groenendijk and Stokhof (1991), with recent developments explored by Sellen (2019). With connections to contemporary spatial semantic frameworks, such as region-based semantics (Brooijmans et al. 2019), the approach is here expanded. First, containment, a core concept in the approach, along with its reverse, is further developed to establish a more comprehensive foundation. Second, the relationship between logical operators, particularly conjunction and disjunction, is introduced within the framework, providing a more structured understanding. Third, the approach is refined by considering how individuals contribute to the overall meaning in terms of reasoning, thus introducing a more dynamic element. Fourth, the approach is further developed by introducing an additional dimension that captures individual perspectives, resulting in a more nuanced framework. Fifth, the approach is refined by introducing a new dimension that captures collective perspectives. By integrating these new dimensions, the approach is now presented in its most refined and comprehensive form.

Reward learning from a combination of human feedback and reward models can be a reliable method for training reward models. However, the process often suffers from the high cost of incorporating human feedback. A key factor contributing to this cost inefficiency is the current approach of comparing individual pairs of responses, which can be optimized by implementing a batch comparison strategy. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages both human feedback and synthetic reward signals within a batch comparison framework. Specifically, we develop a policy gradient estimator that utilizes a semantic guard, which filters out uninformative feedback, and design a sampling strategy to prioritize comparisons with a high likelihood of providing valuable signals. Our approach has been evaluated in a lego design task and demonstrates a significant reduction in human queries per reward update, while achieving comparable performance to using human-only feedback.

The Smyth powerspace construction, a dual to the Hoare powerspace construction for core-compact spaces, is examined in this study. It has been found that the Smyth powerspace does not necessarily maintain core-compactness. However, under specific conditions, such as when the original space is locally compact and bicomplete, it is found that the Smyth powerspace of that space is indeed core-compact. The proof for this conclusion relies on a relevant characterization of core-compactness. The study further investigates under what types of spaces the Smyth powerspace core-compactness can be achieved.

In two-dimensional, three-dimensional spaces, ensembles of looped pointed vortices are analyzed using a modified configuration space where the enclosed area becomes a key factor. This method allows for precise calculation of pressures within these loops, revealing that variations in vortices orientation significantly impact pressure variations, especially in three-dimensional spaces. Notably, thermodynamic properties of vortices behave differently in lower-dimensional (two) versus higher-dimensional (three) environments, emphasizing complex fluid dynamics differences. Research also identifies a direct correlation between minimum energy state and minimal enclosed area in both scenarios, while distinguishing structural disparities in vortex loop configurations between two- and three-dimensional spaces.

The double machine learning approach has gained popularity for achieving accurate variable selection and estimation, particularly through implementations like the double machine learning estimator (AIPW) and Lasso-augmented outcome regression (LAR) which use machine learning algorithms to enhance model performance. Our research compares these estimators under conditions that promote double machine learning method effectiveness, which involve sample size (n), feature count (p), and interaction term count (p0) such that p0 is less than n and p is less than n. These conditions indicate that existing estimators, especially AIPW, may be sensitive to regularization. By theory and simulation, we find that AIPW underperforms relative to LAR in such conditions, especially when p0 is less than n. Our findings suggest that removing regularization from the AIPW estimator can degrade its performance and that LAR is more suitable for such conditions. Our research also provides insights for future research, such as incorporating different penalties.

The $D_s$-mediated tau decay holds significant importance in both the standard model and new physics, and its study on a lattice is facilitated by the relatively recent precise measurement of the tau particle's semi-leptonic decays. A method has been developed and demonstrated to compute the branching fraction of the tau's decay into a charm meson and a neutron using a 2+1-flavor lattice, taking advantage of a maximally twisted boundary condition. This technique takes advantage of the known final-state masses, momenta, and distribution characteristics, and can be applied to decays from a heavy particle of any mass greater than the sum of the lighter particles' masses. A new, independent measurement of the tau's decay constant was made using this technique, and a comparison with previous results from other methods has been obtained.

In a rotationally induced annular fluid space, experiments are conducted with a surface dye and a changing temperature gradient between the inner and outer walls to visualize surface patterns. 
The surface disturbances are linked to rotating baroclinic waves that form due to a non-axisymmetric effect and are visualized through four distinct regimes based on a specific dimensionless parameter. 
A detailed analysis is provided by quantifying wave properties such as wavelength, frequency, and phase speed that are influenced by annulus geometry and relative turbulence intensity. 
The surface patterns are monitored using high-speed photography, translated into a video, and the inner surface is analyzed with image processing to extract the wave's fundamental characteristics.

This research addresses the challenge of modeling and predicting rare events using a Bayesian approach. It focuses on developing a prior for parameters that follow a Pareto distribution, which is achieved by Pólya urn schemes. The study examines two specific models, one of which is novel, and analyzes how a tuning parameter 'm' influences estimation, particularly in terms of incorporating external information. The research also evaluates the performance of these Bayesian models through simulations, comparing them to other methods such as PEV and Bayesian models based on a Generalized Pareto Distribution, in predicting extreme events. These methods are applied to model frequent flooding events in the Mogi-Guaçu river (Brazil) and are validated by an actual case of a flood that exceeded the 500-year threshold.

Building robust artificial intelligence systems that can tolerate significant data corruption is a pressing challenge. Current approaches in reinforcement learning, however, are often constrained to specific types of data corruption or require knowledge of the corruption's extent, which is typically unknown in practice. To overcome this limitation, we develop a general data cleaning method inspired by optimal transport theory, enabling efficient data cleaning for off-policy datasets. We integrate this method with a conservative learning framework, allowing our algorithm to guarantee a certain level of performance without needing to know the corruption's extent. We extend our approach to a decentralized multi-agent conservative learning algorithm, also providing theoretical guarantees. Experimental results on grid world settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms in various data corruption scenarios, outperforming existing robust reinforcement learning algorithms.

This study investigates the approximate controllability of the impulsive heat equation with varying numbers of jumps, thereby extending research on a specific equation examined by Karafyllis and Krstic. It further explores the approximate impulse controllability of a specific system of equations, which can be seen as a generalization of the equation with a single jump, as explored by Karafyllis and Krstic.

A novel method, known as the two-stage quantile transformation (TQT), has emerged as a leading approach to out-of-distribution detection. Despite its success, the TQT method exhibits certain shortcomings when tested on a recently developed challenge dataset, which reveals that its weaknesses arise from a two-stage design. In an effort to overcome these limitations, researchers have developed an improved technique, T*-QT, that utilizes a novel data augmentation strategy to replace the initial transformation stage in both the TQT and TQT-B methods. Experimental findings demonstrate that this new technique effectively rectifies the shortcomings and significantly enhances performance.

This review provides a detailed examination of the mathematical models that describe the behavior of molecular machines. Research into these models has intensified in recent years due to advancements in single-molecule techniques. The models that describe the dynamics of molecular motors in cells are particularly affected by the influence of currents, which can affect the movement of the molecules. The conditions under which the models are valid and how they can be further improved are also discussed. The analysis focuses on the specific cases of myosin V, kinesin-1, and kinesin-2 as examples.

Consider two types of transducers that operate on input and output strings, 
connected through a shared tape that can be moved back and forth by an 
operational head. As it scans, this head produces output at a specific point 
aligned with the input. However, if the head creates output at a different 
position than its current location, the alignment shifts. When the head 
moves to a new input position, its output alignment adjusts accordingly.

Some special transducers, which only allow the head to move to a new 
alignment after reaching a specific input position, can be seen as equivalent 
to ones that only move forward through the input, without shifting back.
These can be described using a different kind of transducer, aligned with a 
specific new property that can be recognized and understood through a 
important relationship between languages and the alignment's eventual effect.
Furthermore, this property enables the conversion of any transducer with 
double-determinism, that can be aligned with input using a limited and 
regular method to adjust its position, into an equivalent forward-only 
transducer. However, this method cannot be easily adapted to work with 
non-deterministic transducers.

It has been shown that converting a general transducer that operates in both 
directions into a forward-only version is a problem that cannot always be 
solved, even when using a bounded, regular alignment method. On the other 
hand, when the desired output can be fully given, a

This research focuses on the efficient calculation of a specific entry in the $f$-Convolution without necessarily performing the entire operation, which is typically more computationally expensive. Currently, a single entry is calculated at a cost of $O(n^2)$, but our proposed algorithm reduces this cost to $O(n\log n)$. As an application, this optimized approach enables the faster computation of a crucial step in a $O(n^2)$ algorithm designed to identify the maximum-weight empty convex polygon in weighted point sets.

Our knowledge of formation processes for intermediate objects between planets and stars is expanding rapidly, thanks to recent discoveries in exoplanets and brown dwarfs. Object GJ 229B, with an estimated age of 12.5 billion years, offers a crucial reference point as its atmosphere is the most extensively studied of all L dwarfs. This object's atmosphere has been observed in multiple wavelength ranges since 2005, with initial data suggesting high temperatures and the presence of water vapor. Subsequent studies in 2014 revealed higher temperatures and the presence of methane, with the latest findings from 2016 showing Object GJ 229B can be accurately modeled using standard atmosphere models, thus marking significant progress in understanding the formation and evolution of intermediate objects.

A two-point spectral density method is used to investigate tetraquark states at zero temperature, and also to consider thermal effects. The method is applied to a well-established case, the $B_c$-system, and we find that the spectral density can distinguish between different theoretical models. We also discover that the presence of tetraquark states is sensitive to the choice of decay constants and mass, and that thermal fluctuations may significantly impact the mass of these states.

With the $C\Gamma$-odd component of CP violation in the Standard Model predicted with high accuracy, the search for beyond-the-Standard-Model new physics becomes more sensitive. Furthermore, the prediction of new phases that may arise in couplings between vector-like quarks and ordinary quarks is also discussed. These predictions are particularly relevant as vector-like quarks may be produced at particle colliders.

To simplify complex aerosol transport modeling, we develop an easy-to-calculate well-mixed model that can be compared side-by-side with two more sophisticated models: inflected plane source and Lagrangian stochastic models. Our research involves sim a typical infected person coughing out particles and measuring the concentration of the simulated material around the individual. We discover that despite differences in the advanced models, they all yield similar results to our well-mixed model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our well-mixed model is in excellent agreement with experimental data collected by Max von Laue Institute. As a result, we conclude that our well-mixed model is a reliable tool for predicting aerosol concentrations.

Measurements of nuclear moments in the $^{135,137}$Te isotopes have been made using a precise method involving spin-coherent source technique, resulting in accurate determinations of magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole nuclear transition parameters. These results were obtained without requiring direct knowledge of the absolute gamma ray intensities. Furthermore, gamma ray spectrum simulations have provided valuable insights into the structure of these isotopes. Specifically, these studies offer information on the nuclear structure of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te, including confirmation of a nuclear structure proposed for $^{135}$Te based on previous research.

This article proposes a method for self-stabilizing decentralized exchanges. A trades sequence is possible only if each trade adheres to the corresponding exchange rules. Our research presents a digital verification tool that can independently identify violations in the exchange process. Building on new theorems about unique transactions, we have developed an algorithm to verify transaction validity in linear time. A violation is detected when one transaction enables two different orders. Additionally, we have created an method to make transactions valid in linear time by removing the causally insignificant transactions. Our ideas are put into practice with the CHAP table structure used in Monero wallet software, which we have tested and found to correctly process a large volume of real-world transactions.

This study provides a theoretical framework for the mass predictions of the $F$-wave bottom mesons. Utilizing quark model with quark potential, the $F$-wave light mesons, as well as the $\pi^0(1800)$ and $a_0(1980)$, have been analyzed. The results indicate that the predicted masses of the $F$-wave bottom mesons conform to the Regge trajectories. In addition, the study proposes that three states each for $B$ and $B_c$ pseudoscalars, and $B'$ and $B'_c$ scalars at specific masses can be experimentally observed.

Each periodic pattern can be represented as a two-dimensional grid of cells, with each cell containing an infinite amount of information, akin to an addressable memory cell, essentially functioning as a state. A minimal set of states required to establish the validity of Szabados's conjecture is defined by the lowest number of states. The more intricate the structure of the pattern, the more states are needed. The complexity of a pattern is determined by the minimum number of states required for its valid representation. The conjecture posits that each pattern has a minimum number of states that can be used. This is confirmed. The minimum number of states necessary to establish the validity of the conjecture, as well as the minimum number of states needed to establish the validity of the conjecture in its most basic form, both do not exceed the minimum number of states needed to establish the validity of the conjecture in its full extent. The maximum number of states needed to establish the validity of the conjecture in its full extent does not exceed three times the maximum number of states needed to establish the validity of the conjecture in its most basic form. The maximum number of states needed to establish the validity of the conjecture in its full extent does not exceed nine times the maximum number of states needed to establish the validity of the conjecture in its most basic form, for a given set of minimum number of states.

A versatile method that uses the incoherent positions of finite number of dots to uncover specific dynamics in a dynamical system has been developed. It applies a form of spectral analysis to a pattern created by these dots in a nonlinear system, which helps in identifying key aspects of its behavior. This method has various forms, each with different numbers and arrangements of dots. By analyzing a small area of a dynamical system, this method can also detect global characteristics of its overall behavior. It has been used in several applications, which include predicting the outcome of a known situation within a system and identifying missing components in a specific scenario. This tool has the potential to be applied in areas like using light to control specific aspects of a system and dynamic information storage.

Researchers have long used fitness landscapes to analyze complex systems, and this concept has been applied to various domains, from chess and genetics to sociology and economics. Notably, Kauffman's research on fitness landscapes laid the groundwork for studying landscape topology and its relationship to system structure. The Economic Fitness and Complexity (EFC) method has been used to study a wide range of topics, including player skills, language structure, system complexity, and more. However, there is a limitation in applying this approach to domains with sequential dynamics. Our research overcomes this limitation by using Monte Carlo simulations to create artificial landscapes based on real chess opening move data. Our findings reveal that popular openings are located in high-fitness areas, and more experienced players tend to explore these areas more extensively. The R rank indicator from EFC accurately reflects skill levels, and it is also discovered that these high-fitness areas provide a strategic advantage, as players using these openings tend to outperform others. TheEFC method is thus a useful tool for understanding the structure of domains with sequential dynamics.

Our study explores the possibility of forming a neutron star within a close binary system that has already evolved into a white dwarf. The code we developed, which uses a semi-classical approach, is well-suited for examining the late-stage evolution of such binary systems, which are too intricate for full stellar simulations. The code we have implemented is an enhancement of the one used in previous research on planet formation, and it is well-labeled for ease of comprehension. This code is well-labeled and employs labeled binary matrices to streamline the solution of the relevant equations.

Derive the integrals of motion for second-order differential equations using the method of first derivatives, including application to the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and other models like the Weber and anharmonic oscillators, as well as a general second-order equation with constant coefficients.

Recent breakthroughs in AI-driven shape generation have enabled skilled designers to create complex shapes from basic outline blueprints, such as 2D sketches or basic 3D sketches, by using neural networks to interpret these more simplistic and structured forms. Nevertheless, when it comes to shapes that deviate significantly from smooth, uniform surfaces, such as intricate mechanical parts with sharp angles or hollow spaces, the current AI-driven methods tend to generate simplified, rounded versions of the shape, losing key details.

A new neural network approach is presented in this study to accurately reconstruct a precise, exact 3D shape directly from a set of basic 3D outline blocks by interpreting a set of fundamental 3D polygonal components, thereby achieving high-fidelity output even for shapes with sharp angles or complex structures. Building upon the earlier success of implicit shape synthesis methods, a new technique utilizing a discrete voxel-based grid system is employed to generate a precise, exact shape that matches the desired polygonal blueprint exactly, while maintaining close alignment with the desired polygonal blueprint. 

Our study reveals that when it comes to interpreting basic 3D outline blocks to create detailed shapes, there is a notable distinction between how 2D and 3D blueprints are handled. 

In particular, when it comes to shapes that deviate significantly from smooth, uniform surfaces, such as intricate mechanical parts with sharp angles or hollow spaces, the present AI-driven method outperforms the earlier implicit shape synthesis method in producing accurate, exact shapes

This series of scientific visualizations illustrates the dynamic processes occurring on the surface of HD80606b, a highly eccentric planet that completes an orbit every four days. This particular animation depicts the planet's surface temperature variations and corresponding atmospheric reactions during a single revolution around its star. To account for realistic temperature changes, this depiction employs an adjusted timeline, allowing the atmosphere sufficient time to adjust to shifting surface conditions. Moreover, this visualization extends beyond surface phenomena to showcase the intricate atmospheric interactions taking place at various altitudes.

Our research builds upon a computer simulation of a one-dimensional, one-zone collapse, which has been conducted using a simplified model. This simulation models a one-dimensional, one-cell fluid that contains an infalling fluid and a fixed mass. We have discovered that when the mass profile is adjusted with a small disturbance, the resulting singularity becomes visible. In contrast to the original simulation, these singularities develop within a small area and do not affect the overall structure significantly. Additionally, we propose a method for predicting when such singularities may occur.

A code-based proof has been established for the weak gravity conjecture in relation to extremal black holes within a specific context. The conjecture proposes that in scenarios where gravitational effects are relatively minor, there exists a way to reduce the mass of extremal black holes. This mass can be further minimized by applying an appropriate, non-extremal force. Our proof validates this for extremal black holes in situations where the initial mass equals the extremal mass. The analysis is conducted within a canonical ensemble framework and assumes that gravitational interactions are relatively weak. The proof is ensemble-specific and cannot be directly applied to grand canonical ensembles. Additionally, our work supplies an alternative method for determining the critical value of the ensemble control parameter.

In reinforcement learning, extrinsic rewards are often used to drive training.  However, intrinsically motivated agents generate their own reasons for action, based on personal goals.  Extrinsic rewards and intrinsic motivation can work together to help agents learn.  The problem of combining these two factors is challenging because it can lead to an imbalance in their influence.  To address this issue, we propose a novel method called iSAR, which uses an intrinsic motivation system coupled with a single adaptive loss function.  This function balances the motivation system and extrinsic rewards by adjusting the learning rate of the intrinsic motivation gradient.  The iSAR loss function is based on the Focal Loss, allowing it to focus on the intrinsic motivation gradient with the highest loss.  Through careful tuning, iSAR efficiently trains agents using both extrinsic rewards and intrinsic motivation.  Our method is evaluated on several tasks, and it is compared to state-of-the-art intrinsic motivation systems.  As a result, iSAR shows improved training efficiency, better final performance, and reduced variance.

A newly developed coloured Poincaré gravity is explored to understand the relationship between a model of massive particles and another of massless particles. By introducing a function to colour the gravity's algebra, two different models arise: a massive particle model for one colour scheme and a massless particle model for another. These models are further compared to a particular case of coloured gravity that leads to a model with both massless and massive particles.

Developing efficient parameterized algorithms for directed problems often poses a significant challenge. We will illustrate this difficulty by focusing on three specific problems: finding a minimum feedback vertex set, locating long paths (specifically 'directed' and 'undirected') and 'clique' detection. To overcome this obstacle, we will explore the concept of 'linking' which combines 'filling' techniques with 'coloring' methods. We will analyze how 'treewidth' and 'clique width' influence the efficiency of these algorithms.

Current system architectures for navigation research often rely on a single, continuously updated location, resulting in inefficient memory usage. The MemoNav model addresses this limitation by introducing a state-based area learning approach, where the environment is divided into distinct areas to store navigational cues. A neural network trained via Reinforcement Learning and utilizing Locality Encoding allows an agent to efficiently recall areas' locations when entering new locations. Through this method, agent can bypass unnecessary movements and significantly enhance its navigational efficiency. Additionally, agent can recall up to 80% more information within 100% less frames.

The deployment of future cellular networks, including 5G New Radio, is primarily centered around the use of unlicensed and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequency ranges. However, with the advent of 5G Advanced, a new spectrum option, specifically the 3.5 GHz (3550-3700 MHz) band, is being explored. This area has been utilized by macro cellular base stations for a significant period but is currently experiencing some interference from small cell access points, particularly those utilizing Wi-Fi. Due to its relatively large cell size, the 3.5 GHz spectrum is crucial for providing wide area coverage. To ensure the seamless operation of 5G New Radio in this frequency range, a deep learning-based system for wideband channel estimation has been developed. This estimated channel information is then utilized to design a dynamic beamforming strategy that maximizes the signal strength at the user equipment while beamforming towards the base station, with a specific focus on mitigating the impact of small cell interference.

This article explores various interactions within activator-inhibitor systems that lead to the formation of complex patterns, considering systems that combine short-ranged coupling and a variety of long-ranged interactions. Theoretical models are developed through a framework that incorporates both diffusive and non-diffusive coupling mechanisms, enabling the emergence of spatially heterogeneous solutions. The article specifically examines the harmonic and Coulombic potentials, in addition to a layer-based short-ranged potential, showing that these interactions can be effectively represented as a combination of harmonic and Coulombic potentials. The article also investigates numerical simulations of these interactions in comparison to a standard reaction-diffusion system. The simulations demonstrate a balance between harmonic potential stability and Coulonic potential instability, with the latter leading to pattern formation through a mechanism that involves the inversion of roles between in-phase and anti-phase modes of inhibition and activation. Moreover, simulations employing both harmonic and Coulonic potentials exhibit a variety of patterns resulting from superposition, whereas those employing a single harmonic potential result in the disappearance of patterns. Additionally, differences in spatial structure and intensity are observed between harmonic potential patterns and those of standard reaction-diffusion systems, while correlations between these systems increase with stronger diffusive inhibition.

The dynamics of an initial state under time evolution within specific symmetry contexts can facilitate simplified calculations of operator growth-related quantities. Without the influence of local disorder, these simplified calculations allow for the determination of information density and its temporal fluctuations, as well as the broader spectrum characteristics. By incorporating local disorder, even more intricate terms can be computed, although for now, this is limited to the case of maximum disorder. The approach can also be extended to include scenarios of partially broken symmetry and higher-dimensional systems.

Recent studies of the resonance at 7.65 MeV in 12C, known as the Hoyle state, have uncovered a previously unknown non-sequential decay pathway. This decay directly produces two gamma rays simultaneously, a direct manifestation of the 12C state's spatial arrangement. When 12C decays into two 8Be nuclei, the point source of one gamma ray is randomly distributed within the reaction zone, while the other gamma ray's source is located at one of the two separate 8Be nuclei. A specific type of radiation pattern, or angular correlation, can be observed that is a direct result of this dual decay process.

The presence of intrinsic length scales within brittle materials necessitates a revised approach to crack propagation, particularly in scenarios involving high energy input where a fundamental length scale becomes comparable to the affected region. To address this, scale-invariant models, characterized by several distinct length scales, are analyzed in the context of an elliptical crack in a material with non-uniform elastic properties. The solution involves both in-plane deformation and out-of-plane displacement. When considering a specific type of material non-uniformity, a general method is developed to determine the displacement field, leading to an exact solution for the case of a material with two length scales, which corresponds to a specific type of gradient elasticity. A comparison is made between the displacement field obtained through a scale-invariant model and that of a material described by a different, non-uniform model, highlighting the differences between these two approaches.

The role of causal information within a communication system is evaluated through the concept of channel capacity, taking into account possible information breaches. A communication system's causal state must be concealed from an adversary who holds causal information, and the adversary's impact is measured by the dimension of its channel's causal states. Examples of such adversaries include memoryless sources, a binary erasure channel, and a memory channel with a specific number of hidden states. It is demonstrated that a particular class of optimal encoding strategies can be applied in the face of this particular form of adversary. It is further observed that the causal states of a channel with hidden memory are fundamentally linked to the optimal strategy for encoding.

In a superconducting $BkPt_2Ge_2$ crystal, our research reveals that both spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity exhibit helical node locking, leading to a fully gapped Bogoliubov-de Gennes spectrum as demonstrated by thermal conductivity measurements. Furthermore, the spin-orbit coupling's influence on the topological state persists even in the superconducting state, which is corroborated by multiple experimental and theoretical studies.

The Second Evaluation of Multi-document Fact Checking Knowledge Acquisition Challenge (SEM-TAB-FACTS) is a multi-document fact checking task that involves utilizing structured information from tables within a report. A contest was held on the Platform for Learning and Reasoning (PLR) to evaluate approaches in utilizing structured knowledge for fact checking. The evaluation took place between June and July 2022, with a time limit of two weeks for submissions. The PLR provided pre-trained models along with a set of approaches to be integrated, including using a pre-trained BERT model for feature extraction and a custom-designed matching algorithm. During the contest, a total of 11 groups submitted 26 entries for the contest. The evaluation revealed 11 successful submissions across 4 sub-tasks. The best submission achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.6166, 0.5662, 0.5621, and 0.5461 on sub-tasks 1 to 4 respectively. The best performing submission achieved scores of 0.6408, 0.5862, 0.5744, and 0.5554 respectively using a combination of approaches including pre-trained BERT features, hand-crafted features, and rules-based methods.

We strongly believe that complex numbers are indispensable for formulating Quantum Mechanics. Although this claim may appear obvious, the persistent debate on the topic within physics is a testament to its significance. To provide understanding to those unfamiliar with advanced mathematical concepts, we demonstrate that an alternative formulation of QM using alternative notations does away with the need for complex numbers, but rather relies on the properties of real quadratic fields. Furthermore, we argue that a similar approach is feasible for Special Relativity, the synergy between which gives rise to an even more fundamental framework.

A metric dimension of a metric space $M$ is the size of the smallest subset of $M$ that can accurately measure the distance to every point in $M$. This concept has been extensively studied in the context of metric spaces as well as specific types of metric spaces like graphs. This research focuses on a method of defining the metric dimension of a metric space based on limited geodesic distance measurements, and how these limited measurements can be represented using a threshold value. These limited measurements simulate a real-world scenario in which determining the exact distance to every point in a metric space is impractical due to limitations in measurement instruments. To understand how the limited measurements impact the metric dimension, this research examines three distinct metric spaces: trees, grids, and Euclidean spaces. By analyzing these spaces, we can gain insight into how the limited measurements affect the metric dimension.

A new approach is introduced to address practical issues in geotechnical engineering that arise from one-dimensional unsteady flow of a filtrating liquid. By breaking down complex equations into simpler components using mathematical methods, researchers can simulate and model fluid flow through materials. The method uses unbalanced finite differences to calculate each variable step-by-step. The technique is tested on two real-world problems that involve a time-dependent process and a sudden change in pressure conditions.

This research paper examines the removal of sulfur dioxide in an O3-UV reactor using a packed-bed reactor with 10 mm diameter silica gel beads. The experiment varied parameters including reactor size, residence time, inlet SO2 concentration, inlet O3 concentration, and inlet SO2-O3 molar ratio, and measured SO2 removal in a moist gas mixture at 298 K. A new reaction rate expression was derived from the study. The results show that SO2 removal is influenced by reactor size and residence time. The optimal removal (around 90%) is achieved with a 40 cm reactor and 4-second residence time, using an SO2-O3 molar ratio of 1:8, an SO2 concentration of 500 ppmv, and typical environmental moisture and SO2 levels. The study's findings indicate that SO2 removal is limited by an reaction between SO3 and a water molecule within the reactor. An increase in SO2 or O3 concentration within certain ranges led to an increase in the rate constant of SO2 removal, with an observed 30% increase.

FPGA-based neuromorphic prototypes are being developed to explore various ways of implementing and scaling neuromorphic systems. This paper focuses on examining how different virtual platform segmentation approaches impact simulation speed for large-scale neuromorphic accelerator simulations. Specifically, it explores the effects of placement and routing strategies on simulation performance. Different configurations are compared to understand their influence on simulation efficiency. Furthermore, this study discusses possible strategies for optimizing simulation performance based on current findings.

Decision Trees serve as a clear and interpretable machine learning model, but their effectiveness is hindered by slow prediction times and their tendency to overfit data. To address these issues, we propose Integrating Decision Trees with Nearest Class Prototypes (IDTNP) for both classification and regression. IDTNP combines the predictive capabilities of Decision Trees with nearest class prototypes, allowing for faster inference and improved accuracy. By partitioning the sample space into sub-regions, each associated with class prototypes, the method facilitates rapid prediction. Furthermore, our approach can incorporate various prototype aggregation methods, each with its own advantages in terms of interpretability, scalability, and performance. Experimental results show that IDTNP outperforms traditional machine learning models, including neural networks, while also enhancing interpretability, as demonstrated on synthetic data, the MNIST dataset, and the real estate market in San Francisco.

High-dimensional time series datasets are frequently encountered in various sectors, including stock market and sensor monitoring, where efficiently locating similar data points within a specified time frame is of utmost importance. However, traditional methods employing distance metrics fall short in meeting these needs, prompting the creation of specialized techniques, including family tree series similar (FTSS). Despite their suitability, FTSS-based methods can be overly rigid and time-consuming, particularly with large datasets. The integration of early abandonment within such algorithms yields significant performance improvements. This research delves into integrating early abandonment within the FTSS-based approach, enhancing its speed without incurring substantial precision losses. The proposed method was tested on eight high-dimensional time series collections, demonstrating its effectiveness in time series search with a maximum acceleration of 11.4 times.

Automated feedback systems utilizing code coverage reports can assist students in enhancing their problem-solving approaches, yet their effectiveness is contingent upon how they guide students to prioritize lines of text. Our investigation examines the influence of varied coverage report formats, including detailed and summary versions, and their impact on students learning outcomes. Through an online course, we evaluated the effect of these reports on ten groups of students, tracking their individual progress and final grades. Our analysis reveals that students who received detailed coverage feedback attained a 25% higher overall code coverage, but experienced a 10% decrease in programming grades. Conversely, we discovered that students who received only summary feedback exhibited no difference in code coverage but achieved a 5% improvement in grades.

In machine learning, it is common to utilize black-box classifiers. However, their decisions are often difficult to comprehend. To bridge this gap, surrogate models, particularly those rooted in symbolic methods, can articulate the rules underlying these decisions, thereby fostering trust and transparency. By incorporating constraints, such as robustness, fairness, and preference, we aim to express complex policies that guide and explain decision-making processes. Our novel approach uses surrogate models to inspect and explain not only final decisions but also intermediate representations within trained models. In particular, we examine the role of surrogate models in extracting rules related to decision intermediate representations. Our experimental findings reveal that: (a) rules derived from surrogate models can accurately predict the classifications made by trained models; (b) these rules can also capture the relationships between different categories within trained models.

Over-smoothing is a long-standing challenge with Graph Convolutional Networks, and understanding the cause of this issue can lead to the development of solutions. Research indicates that over-smoothing results from the combination of decreasing eigenvalues and increasing degrees of samples in the target class. This insight into the instability of eigenvalues and the influence of sample degrees enables the design of solutions. A solution involves modifying the spectral radius of customized algorithms and balancing the degree of samples in each class. This leads to a new algorithm called Balanced Repeated Squaring Graph Convolution, and further improvements can be achieved by applying a new technique called Adaptive Degree Normalization.

Researchers have set constraints on the production of dark matter particles at
frequencies ranging from to 1000 Hz through a detailed analysis of data
collected by the Advanced LIGO detectors. This research establishes the
best-specified limits on four simplified models involving a mediator,
including both vector and scalar types, in a comprehensive framework that
accounts a broad range of interactions between dark and normal matter.
The primary focus of this research is on the bounds set for cross-media
processes a broad range of frequencies, ranging of to 1000 Hz.
We present the bounds set on model parameters, represented as functions of mediator
mass, for four simplified models based in vector, scalar, and two other interaction
types, in terms of normalized coupling.
These new constraints improve significantly upon previous limits set by other
experiments for mediator mass less of 10 GeV.
We also establish a range for cross-sections of dark matter介子 production,
ranging from to 10-24 cm2/GeV, which are set for various normalized coupling
values.
We write code that can calculate these new limits on cross-sections, which are set
using the Advanced LIGO data.
This code is available on GitHub and can be used to set bounds on dark matter
production for an arbitrary frequency range.

We introduce two novel functions that are linked to the transverse movement of partons within hadrons. These functions are carefully designed to be gauge-invariant. We then relate them to a specific quantum effect, known as the spin-orbit interaction, which is facilitated by a specific mechanism. We also discuss the potential to test these functions through a process involving the production of a Z-boson and a jet, particularly by analyzing the junction of parton transverse movements in a specific region of momentum distribution.
