Infinitesimal invariant differential forms play a significant role in the stable cohomology of the group GL(n,R), particularly in the context of its cohomology with a particular degree constraint. Researchers have employed a strategic approach by linking these invariant forms to the algebraic structure of GL(n,R)'s cohomology through a concept known as a Dyer-Laxdin (LD)-action. This connection enables an examination of the spectral properties of the LD-algebra. Building upon the cohomology's structural understanding, they further explore its internal composition through the lens of LD-morphisms. Key spectral and internal structural properties of GL(n,R)'s cohomology have been the subject of a comprehensive study.

A critical issue in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and other deep learning models is avoiding auxiliary variables that can degrade performance. We investigated how deep learning techniques can be applied to RNNs that incorporate auxiliary states, which are essential for processing sequential data like speech and visual recognition. The performance of our RNN model, comprising a complementary set of auxiliary variables, outperformed other state-of-the-art models in classifying CIFAR-100 images, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 79.3%. We also explored different RNN architectures, including those based on LSTM and GRU, and conducted experiments to verify our theory. The detailed analysis revealed the significant impact of auxiliary variables on overall model performance, highlighting their importance in sequential data processing.

The non-Hermitian skin effect causes bulk states to gather at the boundary even after accounting for non-Hermitian biorthogonality.  Understanding how skin effects arise in different types of chains is a crucial area of study.  In a simple non-Hermitian chain called the extended Hatano-Nelson chain, correlations do not contribute to skin effects when accounting for biorthogonality.  However, including correlations in more complex systems results in a significant amplification of the skin effect.  Researchers found that including correlations in the extended HN state increases the skin effect by 10 to 100 times.  To explain this, a new type of symmetry known as $\mathcal{CP}$ symmetry has been introduced.  This symmetry encompasses not just individual particles but also pair correlations and exhibits an unusual property where it is invariant under transformations that change the direction of time.

A QGCA pair with spacing $L$ can be created using a QGCA of length $L/2$ in combination with a binary complementary array of length $L/2$. It has been demonstrated that a QGCA pair with spacing $L$ might not exist even if a QGCA pair of length $L$ is possible. This limitation arises from the constraints imposed by minimum lengths imposed by QGCA construction techniques. In this paper, a novel method is developed to construct QGCA pairs that exceed these constraints. It is shown that a binary complementary pair with length $7$ results in a QGCA pair with length $7$; that a QGCA of length $13$ yields a QGCA pair with length $13$; that a QGCA pair of length $9$ is feasible; and that a QGCA pair with length $10$ is feasible.

Recent data from the LHC's 13 TeV run, specifically from the CMS experiment, have been utilized to establish limits on the Higgs boson's unusual couplings to vector bosons. This research presents the outcome of a combined analysis of several processes involving the Higgs boson, including its production coupled to its decays into vector bosons, in conjunction with its scalar or pseudoscalar decays. Furthermore, this study sets a comprehensive set of restrictions on the Higgs boson's couplings to fundamental particles, vector bosons, and a variety of other particles. Under the assumption that the Higgs boson behaves according to standard model predictions, more precise limits are established on fractional couplings to these particles. The findings indicate that experimental limits on the anomalous Higgs boson vector boson couplings are within the range of standard model expectations, while no significant evidence was discovered for the Higgs boson decaying into other particles.

Unsupervised change detection has several benefits over supervised methods, primarily due to its ability to operate with minimal labeled data. However, it presents a challenge as it necessitates modeling multi-temporal remote sensing images' complex statistical characteristics. To address this issue, we propose an innovative and effective deep learning approach that leverages the autoencoder's capability to efficiently compress image information. By utilizing an attention mechanism, we further minimize the amount of required labeled data, thereby improving the model's capacity to discern statistical patterns in image data. Through thorough evaluation on various datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existingChange Detection approaches, and its synergy with supervised training significantly surpasses both unsupervised and baseline change detection methods.

We establish that for any positive integer n, any subset A of the set {1, 2,..., n}, there exists a subset B of the set {1, 2,..., n} such that the union of the sets represented as sums of up to k squares from A and up t elements from B covers the integer n for all values of k and t. Previous work established a lower bound of n^(1/4), which was improved to n^(1/3) and further refined with a previous study showing that the constant 1/8 could be replaced with 7/16. This current work enhances the previous study by replacing 7/16 with 1/4. It is obvious that for any subset of size exceeding n/2, the representation of every natural number as the sum of two integers is possible, making 1/2 a natural threshold for this problem.

In a Heisenberg spin exchange coupling system, two silicon lattice sites connect via an Heisenberg spin exchange interaction that can be modified by varying the distance between them. Incorporating a dopant atom within the silicon lattice significantly influences this interaction by altering the wavefunction overlap between two qubit states, which in turn controls the magnitude of the interaction. Our research focuses on determining the most effective dopant positions within the silicon lattice by examining how these dopants affect the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction when located at various positions relative to a donor and a silicon lattice site that hosts a qubit. Our findings indicate that dopants positioned within a certain radius around a qubit state maximize interaction strength, while a specific dopant configuration can yield a desired level of interaction connectivity.

This research introduces a lightweight C library, LibOPT, that supports global
optimization through a flexible and modular implementation. The library encompasses
49 benchmark functions, an array of widely accepted test functions in optimal
control, and three predefined initial point generation techniques. Additionally,
LibOPT integrates six established global optimization algorithms. Users can easily
customize the library by combining initial point generation methods, stop criteria,
and optimization algorithms. Furthermore, LibOPT is accompanied by a detailed user
manual and thorough documentation. Users can compile and link portions of the library
to their own projects, allowing for significant flexibility. Our findings indicate
that LibOPT outperforms or matches contemporary, widely adopted optimization
libraries.

We have determined the transitivity degree for complete linearized logarithmic $3$-forms defined on smooth algebraic $3$-varieties within the categories of algebraic varieties defined over a field with a trivial valuation, polynomial varieties over a discrete valuation ring, and algebraic $3$-varieties on a smooth, proper $3$-scheme over a discrete valuation ring with a smooth special fiber. Our results demonstrate that the general transitivity degree equals three, which is one less than the dimension of the underlying algebraic variety, for cases one through three. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound on the transitivity degree for any complete linearized logarithmic $p$-form, where $p$ is a prime number, defining it to be at most $1+\lfloor \frac{p-2}{p+1} \rfloor$.

A crucial aspect of quantum mechanics is the notion of total momentum, applicable to multi-particle systems. This concept also extends to other conserved quantities, such as angular momentum. In this article, the total momentum operator for multi-particle systems is defined within non-abelian frameworks. The operators for individual particle momentum are then specified, taking into consideration position operators. It's noted that in position-momentum space, translation operators for different particles do not commute. The relationship between the momentum operators of multiple particles and their respective position operators is defined by a set of novel, interpretable operators, which can be applied to other contexts as well.

The article investigates the two-photon absorption process within a type II semiconductor quantum well structure composed of a quantum well sandwiched between a bulk material. When two photons interact with the quantum well, an excited state is generated which then decays rapidly into a mobile charge state. Due to the inherent properties of this system, it is possible to generate a single charge carrier from two absorbed photons, resulting in enhanced efficiency. The study explores how recombination within the quantum well can be utilized to improve the efficiency of photodetectors and solar cells.

The rise of large, pre-trained models in NLP has led to a lack of transparency in neural network decisions. This has particularly affected the task of identifying misogyny in text, which is crucial for understanding and combating gender-based hostility online. Misogynistic content is often subtle and requires a deep comprehension of the underlying meanings. Current approaches to detecting misogyny, however, struggle to provide a clear explanation of their decisions. In this study, we introduce Misogynist MARBERT (MAMBERT), a marker-assisted, transformer-based model that can accurately and interpretable identify misogyny in text. By incorporating a separate marker-assisted component, our model can pinpoint the specific words and phrases that contribute to classifying an article as misogynistic. When tested, MAMBERT achieved a 6% higher accuracy than the best non-interpretable approach, along with 16% better F1-score. Our model outperformed the markelr baseline with a 14% higher F1-score, and we demonstrate its ability to accurately identify misogyny in text across various datasets.

The existence and uniqueness of solutions to a type of equation, called the backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE), is investigated when its generator incorporates past values. This novel approach to BSDEs can be applied to study backward stochastic control problems.

Reinforcement learning via simulation is a highly effective technique, yet simulations often struggle to accurately reflect real-world scenarios, particularly when controlling robotic manipulators. Enforcing a minimum threshold on the noise level within the dynamics model in our method leads to the creation of policies that are more resilient when transferred to real-world applications. We enhance the existing world model-based reinforcement learning approach by adding a feature to the dynamics model that accurately predicts a lower bound on prediction noise. We use this lower bound to shape the goals of the planner, resulting in more robust control of the planner. We present two methods for estimating this lower bound: one based on the energy distance and another rooted in the variational autoencoder framework. We integrate our method with world model-based reinforcement learning techniques, called Dreamer, and evaluate the robustness of the controlled systems. We find that our method's simulated policies exhibit high robustness in the following: policies that enforce lower bounds on the noise level within the dynamics model are more resilient to unexpected variations in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we discover that using an optimized world model along with enforcing a lower bound on the noise level yields the most effective results.

We study a distributed caching problem, and have developed a framework that maps caching schemes to combinatorial structures, yielding several key results. First, we establish connections between previously proposed subpacketizing and non-subpacketizing caching schemes and specific Reed-Muller and constant weight codes, respectively. Next, we find that the size of a caching scheme is equivalent to the rank of an associated code. Finally, our framework enables a unified proof that non-subpacketizing codes can be at most of dimension $O(\log K)$, and reveals that any code meeting the minimum distance requirement has a dimension of at most $3$, which implies any optimal caching scheme may be subpacketized with a packet dimension of at most $3$.

We define a predicative version of Scott's model for System F and prove that it is sufficiently comprehensive to System F in a predicative setting. This finding is significant because it demonstrates that Scott's model can be considered a valid constructive and predicative model for System F, resolving an open issue in the field.

We provide a concise reasoning for a formula that expresses the sum of DGEEs associated with Weyl group cosines of the congruence subgroup $\Gamma(p^k)$ as $z$ approaches zero. This approach may also be applicable to other types of Eisenstein series on congruence subgroups of arbitrary levels.

Designing collision avoidance strategies for mobile robotic arms in environments rich with detail is a difficult task. Traditionally, agents have used position and velocity data to avoid obstacles, ignoring the arm's spatial layout. However, this approach can lead to suboptimal decisions as it doesn't account for the arm's spatial configuration. To overcome this, researchers have developed a novel control method that incorporates spatial awareness into collision avoidance. This new strategy uses a homeomorphic transformation to map the arm's spatial configuration onto a dimensionality-reduced space, enabling the creation of a value function that considers spatial factors. Building on this, a reinforcement learning-based controller has been developed to navigate the robot through a dimensionality-reduced space, allowing it to capture and utilize its spatial configuration during navigation. Experimental tests using a physical robot arm have shown that adding spatial awareness to navigation can utilize spatial configurations more efficiently and utilize the environment's spatial features more effectively.
