A comprehensive approach to determining fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries is provided, encompassing both global and local (gauged) aspects of field theories like 3d N=4 abelian super gauge theories and 3+1d topological theories. These derived 1-cocycles can be converted into non-trivial 3-cocycles to describe anemorphisms. The approach also connects to known techniques such as T-duality and has potential applications in studying non-invertible higher-form symmetries, with a connection to dualities in 3d N=4 theories being explored.

The concept of colored Petri nets (CPNs) can be formalized using a specific logic, leading to an investigation of the computational properties of this definition. It has been established that the existence of a solution to a linear equation system, where order doesn't matter, is definable in this logic within a particular context. However, the same applicability doesn't hold for order-sensitive linear equations in any structure. Furthermore, under certain conditions, the existence of a solution to a system of order-sensitive linear equations is CPT-definable when the coefficients and fields involved are all finite. Lastly, the visual representation of a specific type of CPN corresponds to a first-order definable structure within a particular language.

This study investigates valence and conduction band compositions in the (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir_2O_7 series through density functional calculations. Valence band structure analysis shows Bi 6s orbitals contribute to all valence bands, with increased Bi content leading to higher Bi s-state character. Downfolded valence band structures aligned with experiments via ARPES. Downfolded conduction bands matched DFT predictions. Analysis indicates Bi's isospectral hybridization with Eu and Ir, resulting in increased hybridization among doped valence and conduction states. These findings offer insights into valence and conduction band formation and the impact of Bi doping on hybridization in this series.

Consider a set-valued mapping $F$ defined on a Banach space that takes subsets of another Banach space as values, with a property called upper semi-continuous, closed and bounded values. The question arises as to whether a set-valued mapping can have a value set that is a convex combination of a compact compact set when it comes to Lipschitz functions for these mappings. We show that such a set of Lipschitz functions exists when the mapping has a property called metrically convex. Furthermore, this outcome can be further improved upon when the mapping has a property called locally convex range, allowing for uniqueness of these set-valued mappings. This leads to a question about whether a set-valued mapping with a property called smooth selection exists when it is defined on a Riemannian manifold and takes subsets of a Riemannian manifold as values, with a property called smooth, convex range. This set-valued mapping exists when it is defined on a Riemannian manifold and takes subsets of a Riemannian manifold as values, with a property called smooth, convex range. To n-tuples (a_1, a_2, ... a_n) with non-negative real numbers are non-transitive if and only if there's at least one subset of these n numbers whose average is greater than the overall average of all the numbers. This article provides an in-depth analysis, particularly for the case where n equals four. It initially identifies every non-transitive 4-tuple pattern by leveraging the concepts of n-tuples being equivalent and dominant. Subsequently, four distinct sub-types of non-transitive 4-tuples, labeled as basic, light, medium, and heavy, are categorized. The relationships between these sub-types are then explored.

A run-time option enables users to adjust the behavior of a program at run-time, allowing for fine-tuned customization. Linux kernel run-time options are notorious for being intricate and difficult to modify, despite offering a versatile mechanism for dynamic adjustment. In our study, we examined the run-time options within the Linux 5.10.6 kernel to identify those unused in static run-time environments. By employing run-time option tracing and cross-referencing it with the kernel's source code, we identified 115 inactive run-time options out of a total of 263. Our findings suggest that obsolete options could lead to confusion, security vulnerabilities, and inefficiencies, prompting us to introduce a new method for eliminating unnecessary options.

A significant aspect of supersymmetric models involving a stable light supersymmetric particle is that these particles can scatter off atomic nuclei. This interaction can be directly detected, and it is a key factor in constraining supersymmetric models. In this research, we have examined how nuclear recoil events from dark matter interactions are influenced by nuclear form factors. We have examined the impact of these form factors on indirect detection through nuclear de-excitation gamma rays following a dark matter-nucleon collision. Our analysis indicates that recoil rates are highly sensitive to small changes in the mass of the dark matter particle. Furthermore, we have found that under certain conditions, a second peak may appear at a mass approximately twice as large. We have also examined how this nuclear recoil rate can be used to detect light dark matter in the mass range of 1-4 GeV. We have found that a signal from nuclear recoils can be detected by several nuclear recoil detectors, including those based in a liquid argon time projection chamber and a liquid scintillator.

Achieving long-distance quantum communication is a critical requirement for the expansion of quantum information networks. A pivotal element in this process is the distribution of entangled photons, which facilitates the teleportation of quantum states. In this context, our research explores an innovative approach to quantum teleportation by utilizing entangled anti-polariton qubit states as the resource channel. Experiments were conducted to measure the fidelity of this process, yielding a maximum fidelity of 73.1%, which significantly surpasses the classical fidelity limitation of 2/3.

A telemedicine solution is proposed that enables extraction of inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals at a distant patient location.  The solution involves using a combination of deep-learning techniques to track R-peaks in the ECG signal and a machine learning model to account for signal transmission distortions.  By using a dataset of normal heart rate recordings with simulated transmission errors, the accuracy of the deep-learning-based Rpeak extraction is validated.  The results indicate significant improvement in tele-extraction accuracy over conventional methods.  A robust data collection framework has also been developed to enable the training of a machine learning model to account for signal transmission distortions.  The performance of this model is evaluated using real-world and simulated datasets of electrocardiogram signals.  Significant correlations have been observed between the predicted and actual IBIs in the test sets.  The accuracy of the solution has been validated against conventional methods and initial clinical trials have also demonstrated a high level of correlation between the tele-extracted IBIs and actual patient heart rate data.

We present a precise analytical framework for evaluating the effective temperature within active systems governed by stochastic active Brownian motions under the influence of weak active forces. These forces operate under either harmonic or anharmonic potentials. Utilizing these ETT values, we can assess the time-dependent fluctuations and observe distinct behaviors under harmonic versus anharmonic potential conditions. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the effective temperature serves as a reliable indicator for identifying phase transitions and may serve as an early warning signal, providing valuable insights into systems nearing a critical transition.

Developing high-quality 3D models of human expressions is crucial for applications like gaming, virtual reality, facial recognition, and facial analysis. However, the process of creating these models is time-consuming and requires in-depth knowledge of 3D modeling. To address this challenge, we introduce a method called HUMBI, which allows individuals without 3D modeling expertise to develop realistic 3D models of human expressions using a single image. By combining a translation technique and a deformation approach, HUMBI translates a front-facing image into a neutral pose and then creates a detailed deformation model. This method enables the generation of photorealistic 3D models, where a single image is converted to a detailed 3D model with a neutral expression, and then the surface is accurately deformed to match the expression. To evaluate the accuracy of the generated 3D models, we compare the resulting meshes to ground truth data, and experimentally verify the effectiveness of our method.

Language models are increasingly being used to translate between languages, but training a multilingual model from scratch is a costly endeavor, particularly when dealing with multiple languages. The recently proposed frameworks, such as Zero-Shot Translation, attempt to overcome this challenge by leveraging a pre-trained encoder, however they are limited to handling languages that are similar to the ones used in the training data. This paper introduces a new framework, called Zero-Shot Multilingual Translation, which is designed to tackle translation tasks across a wide range of languages, including those that are not present in the training data. This approach is based on a novel framework, called Constrained Sequence-to-Sequence, which is a general solution to translation problems. It uses a pre-trained encoder as a multilingual language model to generate constrained translations, which are languages that are limited to a specific set of options. This constrained translation task can be treated as a few-shot learning problem, which is a type of learning that requires very little labeled data. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated on a diverse set of 20 languages, including languages that are not present in the training data. The results show that the proposed framework is able to achieve competitive translation performance on this wide range of languages, including languages that are not present in the training data.

BasicVSR++ is an enhanced version of BasicVSR that we developed, and it has been integrated into the MMEditing project for open-source availability. We have made several key improvements to BasicVSR++ that have led to better performance. Specifically, it outperforms the original method by achieving a 0.32% higher PSNR and 1.67 madd less FLOPs per frame on the VIDEOVSR benchmark. Additionally, we have explored the impact of different feature fusion approaches, and found that cross-layer fusion yields the best outcomes.

Reinforcement learning has made significant progress in solving multi-task problems, specifically those with a single shared dynamics model.  However, models based on one dynamics assumption maystruggle to adapt to tasks that have different dynamics, which is often a necessity in practice.  To address this, we introduce multi-task reinforcement learning with multiple dynamics models, which allows several models to be trained in parallel within a framework.  These models can be exchanged during training within our framework without compromising performance.  Moreover, we demonstrate through experiments that our approach yields better results than traditional methods, which also involve multiple dynamics models but train them within a single reinforcement learning framework.

A theoretical heat engine is constructed using two thermal heat baths and a set of fast reactions that move towards thermal equilibrium, where the two baths have distinct temperatures. These baths are connected to a network of slower reactions, where the forward and reverse rates are balanced, allowing the system to remain in a state of detailed thermal equilibrium. By scaling the reaction rates by a parameter λ, we can analyze the heat bath temperatures' influence on the heat bath's state. The scaled parameter λ determines the heat bath's entropy and thus the heat bath's ability to perform work. The scaled parameter λ also affects the heat engine's efficiency, where there is an optimal λ that maximizes the heat engine's output power. This optimal λ depends on the conditions of the heat baths and the network of reactions, where it generally remains constant for most reactions but can vary for some reactions where the heat bath's state is more complex. The optimal λ is where the heat engine's efficiency is maximum, where it is limited by the heat bath temperatures' difference. The heat engine's efficiency is also affected by the heat baths' ratio of their conductance, where the heat engine's efficiency is maximized when the heat baths' conductance is in a specific ratio.

Assessing the risk of natural disasters like hurricanes to the power grid is crucial for energy reliability. This research develops a data-driven method to predict how hurricanes affect the power grid by analyzing historical hurricane data that includes the power grid's response. This new approach relies on a database of historical hurricanes and the corresponding impact on the power grid. This research restructures existing data into a suitable format for learning and applies it to evaluate the likelihood of past hurricanes causing similar disruptions in different scenarios. To test this method, it was applied to assess the risk of the Atlantic hurricane season to the Florida power grid. Results from this study indicate that a significant percentage of past hurricanes have caused outages in the region, and there's a notable risk that certain future Category 3 hurricanes could cause outages similar to those caused by past storms.

We prove a higher-dimensional equivalent of Hadamard's three circles theorem for monogenic functions, then build on this to demonstrate a related principle for logarithmically concave monogenic functions across multiple dimensions.

A novel family of piecewise linear maps is introduced, with coding spaces that are algorithmically derived from the Dyck System in formal language theory. Building on previous work by Goggin and Paul for similar maps, descriptions of their future dynamics are developed using states that are analogous to the states in the minimal deterministic automaton for the Dyck System. This framework enables the creation of higher-dimensional generalizations of Paul's maps, with resulting dynamics spatially embedded within a torus.

The primary challenge in modeling complex, semi-regular signals such as spoken language lies in capturing their underlying structures. A solution proposed involves employing a multi-layered quadratic model, which utilizes a sequence of coupled sinusoidal functions to capture the essential patterns within the speech signal. To achieve this, we developed a novel algorithm based on recursive least squares, which is capable of simultaneously training the individual components of this cascaded model. Furthermore, we explored a novel arrangement of these layers, which incorporates both forward and backward connections, and demonstrated that this structure, combined with specific weighting constraints, ensures stable convergence. In contrast to traditional methods that rely on time-based segmentation, our approach enables continuous modeling without predefined boundaries, which may vary over time. We successfully applied this method to the task of spoken vowel synthesis, which involved training a 20-node double-layer cascaded quadratic model and comparing its performance against a standard single-layer version.

This paper introduces a new biclustering-based Collaborative Filtering technique, USBFC, which utilizes adjustable additive biclustering models. USBFC surpasses current biclustering-based CF methods in performance due to its ability to accurately capture the structure of adjustable additive biclustering. A comprehensive method for evaluating the confidence of CF recommendations is also presented, enabling the USBFC algorithm to select the most reliable CFs. Experimental results on large datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the USBFC algorithm.

HD 69833 is a stellar object that appears to be more evolved than the Sun, with a surface temperature of approximately 8400 K. Although it was previously classified as inactive, recent analysis of its activity indicator H-alpha suggests it may actually be moderately active. Combining data from multiple sources, including radial velocity measurements, surface features, and H-alpha activity levels, it is concluded that HD 69833 is likely subject to the influence of magnetic activity from its surface features, possibly causing a moderate degree of variability in its radial velocity readings.

Advanced quantum systems, specifically hybrid superconductor-normal metal nanowires with magnetic coatings, offer promising scalability in exploring quantum phenomena. Specific interest lies in investigating how a zero-energy peak responds to thermal changes and environmental factors. Research utilizing thermal conductance measurements and nonequilibrium methods reveals distinct patterns in zero-energy peaks and dips, which are influenced by various conditions. These findings indicate that zero-energy peaks from non-Majorana sources decrease rapidly with temperature, at a rate comparable to thermal conductance decreases, whereas nonequilibrium-induced features demonstrate prolonged persistence.

Develop a rigorous bicategorical version of topological Hochschild homology, denoted as T(H,X), where H is a homology theory and X is a bicategory with a single object. The definition shows that an initial discovery equates T(H,X) with a shadow of X, which is a universal invariant attached to bicategories. In specific cases, it was found that T(H,X) can be expressed as a colimit of discs within an associated endomorphism category.

Image style has become a key concept in generative art and a challenging topic to tackle. This study explores encoding image style in a compact form by applying an innovation to Color Constancy techniques. A novel approach is proposed that extracts color data from images and represents it as a stylized, one-dimensional sequence of values. This method is superior to traditional techniques like principal component analysis or variational autoencoders. The resulting style representation is then used to classify various image styles and achieve notable success in capturing unique artistic characteristics.

The traditional approach to mapping features in video analysis relies on temporal or spatial positions, but this paper proposes an innovative method utilizing context-ground module attention. The MCGA approach integrates multiple factors, including appearance, motion, and hierarchical structures, to create a more comprehensive mapping. Specifically, the proposed multiple appearance aggregation combines several instances of the same subject from different time points, while motion aggregation captures their relative movements. Additionally, the novel horizontal and vertical aggregation aggregates features from different spatial positions, and the layer pyramidal aggregation handles hierarchical information. All these aggregations are facilitated by a module attention, which assigns a relevance weight to various factors, and the merging process is achieved through weighted sum, making feature mapping a more dynamic and flexible process, and the experiment results in action classification and spatio-temporal classification tasks demonstrate the superior performance of MCGA over the traditional methods.

This research explores how various factors, such as particle Stokes numbers, initial particle distributions, and Froude numbers, influence the settling process of snow particles. By utilizing a specialized 3D Large Eddy Simulation model with an Euler-Lagrange approach, we examine the settling behavior of particles with different sizes and responses to varying buoyancy. Our model compares our findings with data from previous studies, including high-speed video recordings, to analyze particle velocity, concentration, and the formation of clusters. Our study finds that: (1) regardless of our models, the average particle velocity increases as the particle size decreases, with models predicting higher speeds for smaller particles; (2) both models predict higher cluster concentrations as the particle size increases, with varying degrees of accuracy; (3) models predicting higher particle velocities tend to underestimate cluster concentrations, whereas those predicting lower velocities often overestimate them.

Deep learning models have made significant progress in processing real-world data by leveraging the strengths of variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. However, these methods are typically limited to conditional distributions. Our work introduces a novel approach that uses a normalizing flow based on the normal distribution to conditionally generate complex, multi-modal posterior distributions. This framework, Variational Flow Autoencoders (VFE), is built upon a two-stage process: first, an approximate latent distribution is sampled from a simpler, smoother one. By training the parameters of the normalizing flow, we can accurately represent complex conditional distributions. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the VFE in capturing uncertain conditional distributions.

This research introduces a data compression method driven by the need to preserve
outliers in a given dataset. We present a novel approach that employs a
robust autoEncoder, specifically the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE),
which not only compresses data but also effectively eliminates outliers. The
BCAE comprises a pair of networks, a decoder that generates a reconstructed
dataset from compressed data, and an encoder that produces an anomaly-detecting
output. The innovative aspect of our method lies in utilizing two distinct loss
functions, one conventional and the other specifically for detecting anomalies,
to train both the encoder and a subsequent outlier detection module. The
encoded data can then be used for various downstream tasks. The effectiveness
of our method is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments using real-world
data, which showcase its superiority to state-of-the-art data compression and
outlier removal techniques.

We present a novel approach to studying phase transitions using the reduced Feynman path integral generated by an effective action. Applying this method to a system exhibiting phase transition, we demonstrate how it leads to distinct thermodynamic phases. Furthermore, we establish that the path integral's contributions from different saddle points correspond to these different phases and show that the path integral between phases corresponds to coexistence. We also find that each thermodynamic phase is characterized by its own set of active degrees of freedom.

We've introduced a new approach to studying geometric hypergraphs, specifically focusing on convex geometric hypergraphs. In this field, researchers explore concepts of satiation and calculate satiation numbers. A geometric hypergraph can be seen as a set of vertex-hyperedge assignments that adhere to specific geometric constraints, and it is considered satiated if any additional assignment would introduce a forbidden pattern. This framework for studying satiation has potential applications across various fields, such as computer science, signal processing, and statistics. This paper investigates concave geometric hypergraphs - those with concave curves as their fundamental geometric objects - and specifically, circles, to calculate their satiation numbers. This involves determining the largest set of points that can be placed inside a circle such that no subset of points forms a geometric forbidden pattern. This research has significant implications for related fields, such as computer science, signal processing, and statistics.

This study explores the one-neutron removal cross sections of intermediate energy nuclei, focusing on the relationship between cross sections of specific particles, such as alpha particles and deuterons, and their binding energies. Utilizing data from the OSU-Ball experiment with 560, 460, and 360 MeV per nucleon 4He beams on carbon, oxygen, and lead targets, researchers found the cross sections of alpha particles to be significantly greater than those of deuterons. Contrary to expectations, the cross sections of tightly-bound nuclei were lower than those of loosely-bound nuclei. This lower cross section was attributed to the more fragmented neutron wave functions of tightly-bound nuclei. A semi-theoretical model, incorporating these findings, accurately reproduces experimental cross sections.

The Pacific Lamprey, a non-chordate species, demonstrates an extraordinary ability to climb smooth vertical surfaces at 1.1 cm/s using suction cups. Despite the Cupola robot's cup-based locomotion system showing potential for similar applications, its effectiveness has been limited to inclined surfaces. To overcome this, we developed a new approach for Cupola to enable climbing on vertical and overhead smooth surfaces. By incorporating a double-layered actuation system, Cupola can generate sufficient friction to counter its weight. Our analysis shows that a single, rapidly-closing valve provides stable movement, resulting in climbing speeds comparable to the Pacific Lamprey. Cupola successfully climbs vertical surfaces at 1.3 cm/s and exceeds this speed on inclined surfaces. Furthermore, we've validated the applicability of this approach to a multi-robot system by developing a Lamprey-like controller, enabling synchronized climbing speeds.

This study utilizes a data-driven method to develop mathematical models that describe the long-term effects of doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy when used together to treat colon cancer. Using a dataset from a mouse model with colon cancer, we employed a machine learning approach to identify how these drugs influence the disease and the immune system's response. Subsequently, we developed a comprehensive model of the tumor growth and immune system dynamics, taking into account the drugs' effects as parameters. Through this model, we were able to determine how these treatments influence the disease and the immune system's responses. Furthermore, we used this model to predict and validate the effects of various dosing schedules for these therapies. Overall, our model provides a framework for further exploration and understanding of the potential benefits of combining doxorubicin and IL-2 as a treatment option for cancer.

This study investigates wireless communication systems that prioritize minimizing information age rather than just maximizing data throughput. From an information freshness perspective, we derive an optimization framework with complex constraints and non-linear objectives. Utilizing a Lagrange multiplier technique, we break down this framework into two subproblems, which allow us to obtain a nearly optimal solution. Specifically, we analyze single-user and multi-user systems under different channel conditions, including static and time-varying channels. Our findings reveal that higher data transmission rates lead to lower information age. Moreover, dynamic data transmission rates over time yield even lower information age. Additionally, our research shows that multi-user systems with dynamic data transmission rates can achieve lower information age compared to a single-user system.

This research paper explores several aspects related to the conservation of helicity in various contexts. Firstly, it confirms that helicity is maintained across a particular class of weak solutions to a set of fluid dynamics equations. Secondly, it verifies that helicity is preserved in a broader set of weak solutions that may exhibit discontinuities. Furthermore, the study derives a new invariant for a different class of solutions and examines how the approximate solutions generated by a specific method for a type of fluid dynamics equation maintain certain characteristics. About a month after the initial release of this work, the authors discovered that some key findings within it were not entirely accurate. Consequently, the authors have updated and corrected the content of this paper.

Assessments linked to asymptotic behaviors of potentials with compact support in geometrical optics, particularly in two dimensions, are revisited. These re-evaluations leverage refined asymptotic relations, thereby enhancing our analytical approach. Our investigations build upon prior research, such as the work of Faris and Pang, and Trubowitz, and incorporate new, more precise asymptotic formulas. This enhancement leads to a simplified proof of the Hartree-Lin theorem.

Compact binary systems with at least one stellar mass object operate as expected within the frequency range that future gravitational-wave interferometers will detect. These systems evolve over time due to gravitational wave radiation loss, causing their orbital periods to increase. Researchers have developed a model that allows them to estimate the expected distribution of initial orbital eccentricities for these binaries. By using this distribution, it's possible to forecast the eventual eccentricities for various types of gravitational-wave sources. It has been discovered that binary neutron stars will likely be nearly circular when they merge, whereas systems involving a black hole will remain somewhat eccentric even at very close distances. The type of companion star that loses mass before the final merger can also impact eccentricity. Overall, it appears that most compact binary systems will be relatively circular at the time of merger.

A cutting-edge, high-power X-ray free-electron laser (XFELO) is an ideal tool for investigating ultrafast material transformations. To achieve a pulse intensity of around 10^13 photons/mm^2/ns at 1.45 nm, a combination of advanced seeding and undulator tapering techniques will be utilized. The proposed setup involves using a single optical seeding scheme, which enables a 30% energy extraction efficiency, thereby producing a 100-picosecond XFELO pulse. When combined with the effects of tapering, a remarkable pulse intensity of around 10^13 photons/mm^2/ns will be produced.

Event detection in dynamic graphs is crucial for real-world applications, but existing approaches face challenges due to issues like node newness, variable shapes of input matrices and uncertain neighbor relationships. These problems lead to inaccurate event identification. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach called DyGED. This approach uses a dynamic node embedding technique, a multi-set query mechanism, an attention-based neighbor selection method, and a game-theoretic strategy to create and refine local subgraphs for event prediction. To test its effectiveness, we created theogue dataset, consisting of game interaction records from mobile strategy games. Experimental results show that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for event detection in graph data.

For validating hydrodynamic capabilities of computational tools, the self-similar Guderley problem offers a highly non-linear and historically established analytical solution that serves as a benchmark. It describes the behavior of a strong spherical shock wave forming when a point source releases energy periodically into a gas with specific density variations. A given shock energy is released at regular time intervals from a point source that also emits energy with significantly greater intensity in all directions, resulting in a shock wave that repeats itself over a certain period of time. The solution involves a series of equations that can be solved to determine the behavior of the shock wave as time progresses and a self-similar pattern emerges. It has been demonstrated that this self-similar pattern can be obtained within a relatively short period of time and a detailed numerical method for obtaining the solution has been presented. By choosing an appropriate value for a key parameter of the system, a range of solutions can be obtained that are consistent with a wide range of physical scenarios, including those that have been observed in supernova explosions and other astrophysical phenomena. The solutions are characterized by a series of dimensionless parameters that can be used to describe the behavior of the shock wave and a graphing method for obtaining the solutions is proposed.

In the current landscape, numerous Requirements Engineering (RE) practitioners are actively seeking methods to enhance the transparency and interpretability of AI systems.  Explanable AI (XAI) is emerging as a promising approach within this context.  Although research into XAI has gained momentum, there is a pressing need to incorporate its principles into the actual RE processes.  Involving stakeholders in the RE process is crucial for RE's success and executing a RE approach necessitates adherence to established RE practices.  Consequently, there is a significant opportunity for RE practitioners to engage in executing XAI-enhanced RE practices.  In light of this, our research aims to contribute to the community by identifying specific XAI methods aligned with core RE principles and exploring the feasibility of integrating these methods into the RE process.

Colorectal adenomas, a type of polyp with a high risk of transforming into cancer, are often difficult for clinicians to accurately grade, which can lead to a high rate of under-treatment. To improve grading accuracy, researchers utilized computational methods and combined histological data with information from clinical exams and colonoscopies. By creating and standardizing a comprehensive dataset, known as the CADset, researchers trained deep neural networks to analyze digital scans of tissue sections, allowing for the classification and grading of adenomas. When tested with independent datasets, the models demonstrated a high level of accuracy in distinguishing between different types of colorectal adenomas, significantly outperforming conventional methods used during clinical exams.

A specific type of source coding problem has been identified where the amount of data that can be compressed while keeping the number of possible output options fixed has a direct connection to the maximum amount of information that can be retained in the code. We have developed a standard method for solving this problem that utilizes relative entropy as its primary measure, then established a solid mathematical connection between this measure and the coding efficiency. Building on this, we have derived more accurate and simplified formulas for the efficiency and error rates in a range of specific coding scenarios. These source coding problems have direct connections to relative entropy estimation and fixed-length estimation. Our study shows that the most efficient way to estimate relative entropy can be obtained through a solid understanding of source coding.

We introduce MrSARP, a novel deep-generative hierarchical model capable of synthesizing multi-scale image data. MrSARP's architecture comprises two interconnected modules: a base model that generates high-frequency image components, and a top-level module responsible for creating low-frequency components across multiple resolution levels. Both modules are optimized through a combined approach, leveraging a conditional variational autoencoder and a conditional Gaussian process. This method enables MrSARP to not only produce image data but also to generate various data conditions, such as image data at coarser scales or parameterized semi-syntactic images. Compared to current methods, MrSARP offers the advantage of generating image data across multiple spatial frequencies and providing a more efficient parameterization of lower-frequency components. This is demonstrated through experiments with hand, patch, and landscape images, as well as a more complex dataset consisting of landscape scenes.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a promising approach for developing algorithms in the near-term quantum era. However, the QAOA involves a complex variational optimization process that is both computationally and experimentally demanding. To address this challenge, we integrate Bayesian optimization with the QAOA, creating a Bayesian QAOA algorithm. By leveraging observations from prior qubit sampling, the Bayesian optimization algorithm can efficiently navigate the QAOA parameter space. Furthermore, we introduce a method for maintaining an approximate posterior distribution and enhance the Bayesian optimization process by incorporating a multi-fidelity approach. We demonstrate the potential of our developed algorithms through a series of case studies, comparing them to the original QAOA implementation and other Bayesian optimization methods in the context of the traveling salesman problem.

We have derived a novel direct approach to identify the intersection points of two ellipses. By employing a direct formula for the root ellipses of two general ellipses, our formula is straightforward and does not rely on numerical methods or provide approximations. The validity of our formula has been verified through specific cases, including the application of Bezout's Theorem and its connections to well-known special cases. Furthermore, our formula has practical implications in areas such as surveying and robotics, and its benefits are demonstrated through a few illustrative examples.

Actor-critic algorithms are a class of actor-critic algorithms that estimate the policy's expected return gradient by sampling trajectories. The performance of these algorithms is theory-backed but hindered by a computationally expensive density function estimation of the policy's action distribution. This challenge can be bypassed for Gaussian distributions. This research compares four action probability density function estimation methods: one calculates it exactly for Gaussian distributions, another approximates it using the normal approximation method, and for the rest, the variational approximation method and a variational lower bound estimate, respectively. For the benchmark tests on MuJoCo, results show that approximating action probability densities can yield comparable performance to the best approximation for both the action probability densities and the gradient estimation.

We introduce a strategic approach for studying quantum and zero-point fluctuations within the framework of Hubbard models, specifically focusing on systems with pre-existing stripe patterns. This methodology involves employing a mean-field description that's corrected by a quantum fluctuation analysis, which is valid at a quantum level. Our study centers on square-lattice models, where we examine the impact of fluctuations on systems with either triangular or diamond structural distortions. We analyze both the quantum kinetic effects and the zero-point potential on the moving stripes, discovering that quantum fluctuations can stabilize these structures in ways that classical simulations fail to depict.

A novel deep learning approach using a multi-task learning strategy is introduced to tackle the challenges of vertebra identification and localization within sagittal spinal MRI images. By simultaneously utilizing two loss functions, this method effectively addresses both tasks. Building on this, a novel technique was developed to automatically determine the starting slice for vertebra identification, which was then applied in a sliding window fashion to scan through the entire image series. Experimental results from a competition dataset demonstrate the efficacy of this method, with improvements of 8.75%, 10.75%, and 12.5% in terms of various performance metrics compared to the second-best method.

This article introduces a unified mathematical framework for analyzing both the dynamics and geometric properties of large-scale Markovian models, such as those found in random networks and the phase transitions of thermodynamic systems. By leveraging the algebraic and topological structure of these models, specific calculations for determining asymptotic averages and correlation integrals can be simplified. To accomplish this, the relationship between continuations of Markovian dynamics and the algebraic structure of their associated Lie algebras is examined. Furthermore, the connection between the continuity of these dynamics and the topological properties of their associated chain complexes is explored.

We have developed a multi-point duality theorem for toric complete intersections with smooth divisors. This finding implies that the relative I-functions of these intersections exhibit a particular symmetry, with one side a transformed version of the other. This was proven by establishing a novel relationship between the divisors involved.

This study investigates how piezoelectric materials interact when in contact with a piezoelectric fluid. We derive a Complementary Piezoelectric Condition (CPC) that must be satisfied at the interface between a piezoelectric material and a piezoelectric fluid for the existence of non-trivial solutions to the associated boundary value problem. Furthermore, the Copeland surface is shown to be a necessary and sufficient condition for the CPC to be satisfied on a piezoelectric material's surface. We also present a method for constructing a Copeland surface from an existing non-Copeland surface.

A polariton field is typically manipulated within a planar microcavity system, 
where the flow of excitation photons can be directed in various patterns 
through the manipulation of a spatially varying light beam. 
This control permits the creation of specific configurations of polariton condensates, 
enabling researchers to simulate and analyze phenomena such as particle interactions 
and charge movements in a precise and versatile manner.

The second most robust candidate for a lost planet, K2-22 b, exhibits an unusual atmosphere and is situated within its host star's intense radiation environment. Due to its proximity and atmospheric composition, scientists suspect that this planet may be losing mass at a significant rate, and as a result, its existence could be short-lived, with a predicted lifespan of just a few million years. This outcome seems to contradict fossil evidence from isotopic analysis, and further research is needed to clarify the planet's mass, loss rate, and evolution.

We investigate the classification of homogeneous polynomials in two variables up to equivalence defined by fiber diffeomorphism of their link fibration. This equivalence relation creates distinct orbits within the polynomial space. It enables a method to assign a topological invariant, known as the invariant tau, to each orbit. Consequently, we develop an algorithm to compute the invariant tau for a given polynomial.

This paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation of the Linq4ds package in Java, 
which facilitates efficient manipulation of multi-dimensional arrays. 
Multi-dimensional arrays are a common data format in Data Analytics, widely supported 
by popular frameworks like C# and Python, as well as Data Science tools such as 
pandas and NumPy. 
Although Java offers the multi-dimensional array type natively, existing Java libraries 
like OpenCV and TensorFlow lack a fully integrated, well-tested package for handling 
them in Java. 
The proposed solution, Linq4ds, provides a similar API to other libraries, but with 
additional support for one-dimensional arrays and a emphasis on performance and reliability. 
To demonstrate the capabilities of Linq4ds, a case study is presented that compares the 
performance and functionality of the package with other Java-based libraries, including 
OpenCV and TensorFlow.

During the 17th century, many scientists adopted Galileo's principle of seeking to discover fundamental properties through observation of nature's phenomena, but an analysis of his actual practices shows that he frequently employed complex reasoning to interpret these observations, which often obscured rather than clarified the nature of these principles, in fact, his success in solving mechanical problems using empirical evidence was minimal.

A quantum system's q-Gaussian distribution is considered. Using a non-standard average, we derive formulas for binding q-energy, entropy, and specific heat in terms of binding q-energy. These formulas demonstrate that the standard system quantities can be obtained as a limit case of the binding q-analogues. Furthermore, we show that binding q-energy can be used to generalize the standard thermodynamic relations. Ultimately, we use this framework to obtain a non-Gaussian generalization of the thermodynamic equivalence principle.

In the field of magnetic island coalescence, a distinctive example of magnetic reconnection is observed. It effectively bridges the large-scale magnetohydrodynamics with the minute details of kinetic behavior. Our research provides a thorough, self-contained explanation of magnetic island formation and coalescence. We outline the various stages of magnetic reconnection and the resulting island formation, as well as a successful 3D simulation showcasing simultaneous island nucleation at multiple sites. We also discuss how island coalescence fits into the broader context of non-linear magnetohydrodynamics and the interaction between different scales of turbulence.

Digital assistants learn and adapt to their human counterparts, similar to how humans learn from one another. In the process, they create their own problem-solving methods and general knowledge, which enables them to handle novel situations. A key challenge in developing these methods is establishing performance metrics that reflect human-like learning and are feasible to implement algorithmically. To address this problem, a novel framework is proposed that incorporates human-like learning by having the assistant and a human co-develop their own problem-solving methods, which are then evaluated in the context of collaboration. By applying this framework to the domain of collaborative route planning, we demonstrate that it leads to improved performance and robustness. Furthermore, we show that it also results in the development of plausible digital assistants that can be evaluated through both automated testing and more subjective human evaluation.
